newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Milosevic promises to halt media crackdown.
newsitem.headline: Milosevic promises to halt media crackdown.

text.p: Yugoslav President Slobodan Milosevic has promised to halt a media crackdown and ensure fair treatment for political rivals in campaigning for Serbian presidential and parliamentary elections later this year.
Milosevic on Thursday met opposition leader Vuk Draskovic who outlined preconditions for his participation in the autumn elections, Tanjug news agency reported.
Draskovic sought multi-party control over the electoral process and access to all the media for opposition parties.
"Milosevic expressed "a positive stand on these preconditions", the agency said.

He did not concede a third demand for an end to state interference in the private media but said new licensing rules for independent radio and television stations could be postponed until after the elections to show "good will".
Draskovic said that Milosevic had agreed to unblock the state media and use his influence to reopen the 55 television and radio stations that have been closed down in Serbia for not having licences.
Despite the assurance, Tanjug reported the closure of three more radio and television stations in southern Serbia.

The United States says a key condition for improved relations between Washington and Belgrade -- which would help end international financial sanctions against Yugoslavia -- depends on improved press freedom in Serbia.
Freedom of the press figured prominently in the platform of huge protests by the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition across Serbia last winter which seriously challenged Milosevic's rule.
Zajedno won local elections last November in Serbia's 14 biggest towns, including the Yugoslav capital Belgrade.
Media control is vital to the ruling Socialist Party of Serbia (SPS) ahead of presidential and parliamentary elections, due by the end of the year.
The vote will pick a successor to Milosevic, 55, who was sworn in as Yugoslav federal president on Wednesday after ruling Serbia for a decade.

The opposition says state-run television, the basic disseminator of information to a population too poor to buy newspapers regularly, has a heavy pro-SPS bias. It has promised to boycott Serbian elections in protest.
Milosevic and the SPS can now afford to be generous to the opposition as it no longer poses a threat like last winter.
